---
name: pull-request
description: Land the ticket on its feature's branch and keep the feature's pull request, up to date, with its continuous integration green, fixing it when it is red. A graph with a gate after this step keeps the ticket's own pull request for the team to review.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

<!-- Generated by Bernard the taktician. Do not edit: change .factory/ and run `bernard sync`. -->

The ticket's change is validated and reviewed. One pull request per feature, the feature's branch to the base branch, is what the team reviews (ADR-0041): this skill opens it or updates it, and gets it green. `bernard pull-request` drives it on the forge the project's config names, through the forge's command-line tool, signed in in this environment (ADR-0036). A project without continuous integration overrides this skill.

How the ticket reaches the feature's branch depends on its request:

- `merge` is true (its graph has no gate after this step): the ticket has no pull request. The command merges the feature's branch into the ticket's, then lands the ticket on the feature's branch, and waits for the feature pull request's checks.
- `merge` is absent (a gate follows): the command opens or updates the ticket's pull request, `branch` to `baseBranch`, which the team merges, and waits for its checks. It opens or updates the feature pull request too.
- `recordsOnFeatureBranch` is true (the pipeline opens a pull request per ticket, ADR-0051): the ticket's record is committed on the feature's branch, never on the ticket's. Add `--records-on-feature-branch` to the command below: it refuses a ticket branch that holds the record, naming its files, and you `git rm --cached -r` them, commit, then run the command again.

1. Read `git status` and `git diff`. An empty change, nothing to land, ends `passed` at once: no commit, no pull request. The change is empty only on the first attempt (`attempt` is 1), when the working tree is clean and the branch holds no commit beyond its base (`git log --oneline origin/<baseBranch>..HEAD` is empty; with `--merge`, beyond `origin/<featureBranch>`). A retry (`attempt` above 1) always runs the command, even on a clean tree: the ticket may have landed already, and the command still waits for the checks. Group the change into atomic commits that each build: Conventional Commits, the module as scope, the tests with the code they test. The `optimise.json` files of the feature folders go in a commit of their own, `chore(optimise): record the analysis of <feature>`. Leave `.pipeline/` alone: the orchestrator commits the ticket's record.
2. Write, in your `handoffDir`, the files the command reads, so that no free text goes on the command line. Describe the goal, not a file-by-file changelog, in lines short enough to scan.
   - `feature-section.md`: the ticket's section of the feature pull request's description, in the shape of `feature-section.template.md`, next to this file: what the ticket does, with its path; how it is tested; and, from the last code review's handoff next to it, if any, the review findings left unfixed and each reviewer that reviewed fewer files than it was given, named as a gap in the review. After a step that ran the `optimise` skill, its last handoff next to it gives the section its table of the causes, each row with the lens that found it and its drafted issues, as the template shows. The command keeps a table of the feature's tickets on top of the description: the sections below it share one shape. Azure DevOps cuts a description at 4,000 characters, whatever the number of tickets: keep the section to a few lines.
   - `feature-closes.md`: the one line that closes the feature's issue when the feature's pull request merges. The command writes it under the plan's path, only when it opens the pull request. The feature has no issue the forge closes: leave the file out.
   - `feature-title.md`: the title of the feature pull request, as the one line it is. It comes from the feature's plan and follows Conventional Commits, `<type>(<scope>): <subject>`, with the request's `featureTrackerKey` as the scope when it has one, such as `feat(DATA-12): export invoices as CSV`: the tracker links the pull request by it. The command uses it only to open the pull request, never to change one: a title a human edited stays. Write it every time.
   - Gate mode only: `pull-request.md`, the ticket's pull request description: what the change does and why, with the ticket's path, how it is tested, and the review gaps as above. And `title.md`, the ticket's pull request title, one line, Conventional Commits with the request's `trackerKey` as the scope when it has one.
3. Run the command from the root of the working copy, with the longest timeout your shell tool allows: it waits for the checks, nine minutes at most. Its options come from your request: `<feature>` is the request's `feature`, and `<plan>` the path of the feature's plan, in the feature's folder, where the project's plan step wrote it.

   ```
   bernard pull-request --base '<baseBranch>' --handoff-dir '<handoffDir>' --merge --feature '<feature>' --feature-branch '<featureBranch>' --feature-base '<featureBase>' --ticket '<ticket>' --plan '<plan>'
   ```

   In gate mode, the command drops `--merge`, and reads the ticket's own title and description from the same folder.

   It merges the base into the branch (ADR-0036), pushes it, then either lands it on the feature's branch by a push that is never forced, merging again and trying again when the branch moved meanwhile, or opens or updates the ticket's pull request. It opens the feature's pull request or rewrites the ticket's section of its description, between its `<!-- ticket:<id> -->` markers, and the table of the tickets, from the feature's record, and waits for the checks of its last commit. It stops at the first action that needs you, with a `RESUME:` prompt: do what it says, then run the same command again. When the pull request it waits on conflicts with its base, it merges that base in itself, once per run, and pushes (the feature's base for the feature's pull request, the ticket's base for the ticket's). A conflict in files stops it on `MERGE_CONFLICT` (exit 3). A pull request still conflicting afterwards stops it on `CI_CONFLICT` (exit 9): run the same command again, which merges the base again. It keeps no state, so running it again is safe.
4. The checks are red (exit 4): follow `ci-fixer.md`, next to this file.

Never push to the base branch.

Done when the command prints `CI_GREEN`: `passed`. A check that fails for a reason outside the code, such as a missing secret or a runner that does not start: `blocked`, naming the check and the reason. `CI_CONFLICT` on the feature's pull request of a `per-ticket` pipeline, which holds only the records and which the command never merges: `blocked`, naming the branch. A red check still red after your round of fixes, under the stop rule of `ci-fixer.md`: `failed` with `ci-red`, giving the failures as that rule says: nothing copied from a log.
